precepts.text: Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, and they shall judge the people with just judgment. Job prepared his seat in the street: he was one of these judges.
precepts.point: If I laughed on them, they believed it not: Job had an austere spirit. I chose out their way: he counseled and directed them. And sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners. Job sat like a king in the army.

note.label: Job Sees America's 250th Anniversary

precepts.why:
“When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street!” What does that mean, he prepared his seat in the street?

“Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.”

So Job was a judge. He sat in the gate and judged the people with just judgment. That is why “The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up. The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth.” When Job rolled on the scene, everybody shut the hell up. Princes covered their mouths, young men moved the hell out of the way, and the old men stood up and saluted him. The nobles held their peace; they had nothing to say either. That is total respect and honor.

precepts.text: Observe the month of Abib and keep the passover.
precepts.point: January is not the new year.

note.label: Pope Nicholas & the Moors of Spain

precepts.why:
Deuteronomy 16:1 is where Moses names the month again with the Passover. It joins the Passover and the month of Abib together, the same as Exodus 13, which says of the night we came out of Egypt, “This day came ye out in the month Abib”. The first month of Exodus 12:2, “the beginning of months”, is Abib, the spring month when the tender barley ears appear.

So the biblical new year does not begin in January. It begins in the spring, at Abib, and each month begins with the moon. January is from the Roman god Janus, who presided over doorways, time and new years.

Who changed it? Daniel 7:25 says the beast “shall speak great words against the most High, and shall wear out the saints of the most High, and think to change times and laws”. The great words are the lies Rome spoke against the Most High: a white man who died for the sins of everybody on the planet, that you must be dumped in the water to be saved, Lent, Christmas and December 25th. Wearing out the saints is the slavery. And changing times and laws is moving the beginning of the year from spring to January, and even daylight saving time. Keeping Abib is coming back to the Most High's times.

precepts.text: Three times a year all males appear before the Lord: unleavened bread, weeks and tabernacles.
precepts.point: Christ went up at twelve for Passover. He was born at Passover and died at Passover.

note.label: The Kingdom Of Adam And The Old World

precepts.why:
Luke says Mary “laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.” The inn is a hotel. Why was there no room in the hotels? Deuteronomy 16:16 shows it: “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles”.

The feast of unleavened bread is the Passover; the feast of weeks is Pentecost. Three times a year all Israel had to go up to Jerusalem, and at that time every inn was full because everybody came up for the feast. There was no room in the inn because it was the Passover.

Christ was not born in the manger. The prophecy in Song of Solomon 8:5 says, “I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth”. Mary brought him forth under the apple tree, and after that took him to the manger, because the city was full for the feast.

precepts.text: Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the LORD in the place which he shall choose, at the three feasts, and they shall not appear before the LORD empty.
precepts.point: Neither shall any man desire thy land when thou shalt go up to appear before the Lord thrice in the year: when the men left their land and went up to keep the three high holy days, the Most High promised no man would desire their land.

note.label: Exodus 34: The Second Tables and the Covenant Renewed

precepts.why:
“Thrice in the year shall all your men children appear before the Lord God, the God of Israel.” The law is written again in Deuteronomy, and it names the three: “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles”.

The feast of unleavened bread is the Passover season; the feast of weeks is Pentecost; and the feast of ingathering at the year's end is the feast of tabernacles. “and they shall not appear before the Lord empty”: each had to bring his sacrifice.

When the men left their land and went up to keep the three high holy days, the Most High promised, “neither shall any man desire thy land, when thou shalt go up to appear before the Lord thy God thrice in the year.”

precepts.text: Judges in all thy gates must judge with just judgment, respect no persons, and take no gift, for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise.
precepts.point: Israel's judges later fell into exactly this: they became covetous and took bribes to clear the guilty and turn aside the poor in the gate.

note.label: Numbers 35: The Cities of the Levites and the Cities of Refuge

precepts.why:
The judges could “take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer, which is guilty of death”, and no satisfaction for the manslayer to come home before the death of the priest. A guilty man cannot buy himself off.

“Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment. Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.”

No matter who stands before the judge or what money is offered, if they are guilty of death they are guilty of death. A gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous, which is why the judge in the gate may take none.

precepts.text: Count from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day the wave sheaf is brought; seven sabbaths shall be complete; the counting law behind the feast of weeks.
precepts.point: Rejoice before the Most High, thou and thy son and thy daughter, thy manservant and thy maidservant, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow; and remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt.

note.label: Deuteronomy 16: The Three Feasts and Just Judgment

precepts.why:
“Seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee: begin to number the seven weeks from such time as thou beginnest to put the sickle to the corn.” Leviticus gives the counting law behind it: “And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete”.

The count begins from the day the wave sheaf is brought, when the sickle first goes to the corn, and runs seven sabbaths, seven weeks. Another name for the feast of weeks is the feast of firstfruits: you count seven weeks and then a day, fifty days, which is Pentecost.

Then keep the feast unto the Most High with a tribute of a freewill offering according as the Lord thy God hath blessed thee, and rejoice before him, thou and thy son and thy daughter, thy manservant and thy maidservant, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow; and remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt.

precepts.text: Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord: in the feast of unleavened bread, which is known as Passover; in the feast of weeks, which is known as Pentecost; and in the feast of tabernacles, which is also known as the feast of booths. Elkanah, who lived in mount Ephraim, was applying this law over and over again.
precepts.point: The man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer unto the Lord the yearly sacrifice, and his vow. What is that yearly sacrifice going into? Deuteronomy 16:16.

note.label: 1 Samuel 1: Hannah's Vow and the Birth of Samuel

precepts.why:
“Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty”.

The feast of unleavened bread is known as Passover; the feast of weeks is known as Pentecost; and the feast of tabernacles is also known as the feast of booths.

That is what the yearly sacrifice is going into when “the man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer unto the Lord the yearly sacrifice, and his vow.” Elkanah, who lived in mount Ephraim, was applying this law over and over again, going up to the place the Lord had chosen.

note.label: 2 Chronicles 8: Solomon's Cities, Service, and Dominion

precepts.why:
“Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty.”

That is the commandment of Moses Solomon kept. He offered burnt offerings on the altar he built “on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, even in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles.” The place the Lord chose was the house in Jerusalem, and there the three feasts were kept as written, with the priests, Levites and porters in their courses by the order of David.

precepts.text: Thou shalt not wrest judgment, respect persons, nor take a gift, for a gift blinds the wise.
precepts.point: There is no point in a fool holding a price to buy wisdom when he has no heart for it.

note.label: Proverbs 17: Trials That Refine and the Weight of Words

precepts.why:
“He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the Lord.” To justify the wicked is to wrest judgment and take a bribe. “Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.”

A bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous, and this perverting of judgment is something we suffer with as a people.

note.label: Acts 6: The Grecians Were Greek-Speaking Israelites

precepts.why:
“Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty”.

This is why devout Israelites came to the feasts from every captivity, and why Greeks were at Jerusalem to worship at the passover. The law called all the males to appear, wherever they had been scattered, and the Grecians of Acts 6 were Israelites keeping that law.

precepts.text: Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Most High, in the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks, and the feast of tabernacles; that is why the eunuch came to Jerusalem to worship, keeping the law.
precepts.point: People say this proves Philip went to the heathen Ethiopians, but this eunuch was a Jew, part of the remnant of Israel scattered in Ethiopia, in Kush, during the Babylonian and Persian captivity. That is why Christians confuse the Ethiopian eunuch; they do not understand Bible prophecy or Bible history. Candace was a real title of the queens of the kingdom of Kush who ruled from the city of Meroe, and the queen of that time was likely Amanitore, around the same period as the famine in Acts chapter 11.

note.label: Acts 8: The Word Scattered Abroad, and the Baptism unto the Conscience

precepts.why:
Why had the eunuch “come to Jerusalem for to worship”? Because that is the law. “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God in the place which he shall choose; in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles: and they shall not appear before the Lord empty”.

He was keeping the law, coming up to Jerusalem to appear before the Most High at the feast. That is a Jew of the remnant scattered in Kush, not a heathen Ethiopian.
